messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: NUTS questions
parts:
Two questions about NUTS that (hopefully) should be easy for someone to answer (Matt maybe?).

1. It seems like it would be useful to bound the number of steps taken in each step.  To do this stopping after a certain tree depth seems like it shouldn't affect detailed balance or reversibility, though I haven't checked through the proofs carefully.  Is this correct?  If so, how do people feel about adding a maximum depth parameter to the sampler?

2. Based on the argument in the arxiv paper, the dual-averaging adaptation of the stepsize should be convergent since H is bounded.  Based on that, is there a reason to ever turn it off?  It seems that the adaptive MCMC convergence results based on diminishing adaption should apply here.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] NUTS questions
parts:
Hi Marcus,

1. Yup, you can bound the number of steps no problem. This is
something we've discussed doing in Stan; the possible downside is that
if you really do need thousands of steps to make any progress then
you'll be more random-walky than you want to be.

2. The thing about those convergence results is that they're
asymptotic. Asymptotically, all sorts of things are true. For example,
you don't need to do a "warm-up" (a.k.a. burn-in) phase, since the
early iterations will eventually be washed out. But in practice, where
we only run the algorithm long enough to get, say, a dozen effectively
independent samples, those asymptotic results aren't so relevant.

Matt

I should clarify #2 a little bit: the issue is that, even though the
bias introduced by the adaptation vanishes eventually, it can be
significant for an arbitrarily long time. Especially with an algorithm
like dual averaging, which is a little more responsive in later
iterations than simple Robbins-Monro is. In my experience, the most
serious consequence of leaving adaptation on is usually samples with
wrong (usually inflated, IIRC) variances, rather than seriously wrong
means.

Matt

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] NUTS questions
parts: On Wed, Mar 14, 2012 at 7:13 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:

Hi Marcus,

1. Yup, you can bound the number of steps no problem. This is
something we've discussed doing in Stan; the possible downside is that
if you really do need thousands of steps to make any progress then
you'll be more random-walky than you want to be.

Of course, but there is a flip side.  Once the sampler has "mixed" (assuming it ever really does...) completely independent samples may be less valuable than multiple, mildly independent samples when computing expectations.  For instance, Radford suggested using the entire simulation trajectory (weighted using an alternative acceptance function) for estimating expectations.

As Andrew mentioned, there is a real possibility of a (practically) infinite loop.  For instance, it's not inconceivable that NUTS finds a periodic orbit and is never able to terminate.  Would anyone object if I add this functionality?  I'm happy to have it default to off.

2. The thing about those convergence results is that they're
asymptotic. Asymptotically, all sorts of things are true. For example,
you don't need to do a "warm-up" (a.k.a. burn-in) phase, since the
early iterations will eventually be washed out. But in practice, where
we only run the algorithm long enough to get, say, a dozen effectively
independent samples, those asymptotic results aren't so relevant.

True, but basically every (practical) MCMC result is asymptotic.  And, to be clear, I'm not arguing against a warmup or burnin phase.  Rather, I was just wondering about leaving the adaption on after the burnin.  However, your point (in your next email) about inflated variance is fair enough.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: NUTS questions
parts:
Wow, a lot happened on the list since earlier
this afternoon!

Marcus -- please feel free to add a parameter to
bound the max number of steps. It's kosher from
a detailed balance perspective.

The decision we need to make is what to set as
its default value.

Making it too small runs the risk of reverting
to more random-walk-like behavior and therefore
reducing effective sample size. There's no
risk of periodic cycles due to the U-turn criterion,
so it doesn't technically go into an infinite loop.

Having said that, a default value like 2**20 (1M
or so) seems excessive, whereas 2**8 (256) seems
too small. I think it should be 2**12 or so.

The problem with making the bound too small is that you
can get more random walk-like behavior without any warning.
Making it too large and it can seem to hang, but at
least you get some feedback that it's having trouble
moving.

Ben's belief is correct -- setting the number of steps
turns off NUTS and reverse to a fixed step-size HMC. You
can turn on/off step-size adapation (and presumably
mass matrix adaptation when NUTS II is in) independently
of turning on/off NUTS.

Following Radford's advice (in both the MCMC Handbook paper on HMC
and his response to the NUTS paper on his blog), I added the
option to randomize step size (even after adaptation), which is
also kosher for detailed balance. This can be turned on
independently of NUTS, though Matt doesn't think it'll be necessary
for NUTS.

As to using all the steps of the trajectory, I don't know
how that would play with detailed balance -- you may
need to restrict to samples meeting the slicing criterion.

It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
(from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
is that this should improve the effective sample size
(at least for estimating the mean).

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: NUTS questions
parts:
Regarding using the entire trajectory rather than just a single point
along it, this can't possibly hurt (I think), and is indeed kosher.
(Although you have to get a little bit subtle to actually prove it.)
But I wouldn't expect it to improve effective sample sizes much at
all, at least for problems where the ESS is significantly less than
the number of iterations. The reason being that the autocorrelations
within a trajectory are going to be pretty enormous. And in the
scenario where it takes many iterations to explore the energy
distribution, taking more samples within a given energy level isn't
going to help with that at all.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: NUTS questions
parts: On Wed, Mar 14, 2012 at 7:54 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Wow, a lot happened on the list since earlier
this afternoon!

Marcus -- please feel free to add a parameter to
bound the max number of steps.  It's kosher from
a detailed balance perspective.
Ok, will do.  I've already added such a parameter to nuts_sampler.  I just need to add a setting interface and command line parsing for gm.

The decision we need to make is what to set as
its default value.

Making it too small runs the risk of reverting
to more random-walk-like behavior and therefore
reducing effective sample size.  There's no
risk of periodic cycles due to the U-turn criterion,
so it doesn't technically go into an infinite loop.

Having said that, a default value like 2**20 (1M
or so) seems excessive, whereas 2**8 (256) seems
too small.  I think it should be 2**12 or so.
2**12 = 4096 is a large number of steps compared to what most people have used in practice with HMC before.  It seems reasonable to me, but we could be more conservative and go with 2**16 = 65k.

The problem with making the bound too small is that you
can get more random walk-like behavior without any warning.
Making it too large and it can seem to hang, but at
least you get some feedback that it's having trouble
moving.

Ben's belief is correct -- setting the number of steps
turns off NUTS and reverse to a fixed step-size HMC.  You
can turn on/off step-size adapation (and presumably
mass matrix adaptation when NUTS II is in) independently
of turning on/off NUTS.

Following Radford's advice (in both the MCMC Handbook paper on HMC
and his response to the NUTS paper on his blog), I added the
option to randomize step size (even after adaptation), which is
also kosher for detailed balance.  This can be turned on
independently of NUTS, though Matt doesn't think it'll be necessary
for NUTS.

My experience has been that the randomized step-size can be rather helpful in finding (and escaping) from narrow parts of the energy landscape where the local curvature is high or changes significantly.  I don't see how this wouldn't be the case with NUTS.  It's probably not the case with an RMHMC type simulation, but who knows.

As to using all the steps of the trajectory, I don't know
how that would play with detailed balance -- you may
need to restrict to samples meeting the slicing criterion.

It doesn't impact detailed balance at all as the sampler proceeds in exactly the same way.  The only difference is you keep around the simulation trajectory and a weight which is equal to the probability of accepting that state.  See "An Improved Acceptance Procedure for the hybrid Monte Carlo algorithm" by Neal in J Comp Physics (1994) which discusses this in the context of Neal's windowed acceptance function.

It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
(from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
is that this should improve the effective sample size
(at least for estimating the mean).

If you're thinning then it's not worth doing this, as the trajectory will be less useful than the thinned samples.  On the flip side, since the NUTS trajectories tend to be long, there seems to be less cause to thin in which case the simulation trajectory could provide some useful information.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: default NUTS steps; avg steps/thinned samples
parts:
If we set the maximum number of steps to something
too small, the danger we face is that the algorithm
will give the appearance of sampling just fine, but will
actually have random walk behavior. A bigger danger is
that the convergence diagnostics will think everything is
OK in this situation. I could easily see that happening
given the Metropolis example in the NUTS paper.

If the model is well behaved, there's no problem with
a large number of steps because we'll never get that far.

If we set the number of steps to something small,
we'll definitely need send up red flags when we don't hit
the U-turn condition in NUTS. That way, at least
the user would know something's going wrong. In fact, we
should do this either way, because even 64K steps may
be too few in some situations (hey, we wanted to run
very complex models -- they may still be pretty slow).
And it'll be a good diagnostic to see.

>> It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
>> thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
>> (from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
>> is that this should improve the effective sample size
>> (at least for estimating the mean).
>>
>> If you're thinning then it's not worth doing this, as the trajectory
>> will be less useful than the thinned samples. On the flip side, since
>> the NUTS trajectories tend to be long, there seems to be less cause to
>> thin in which case the simulation trajectory could provide some useful
>> information.
>>
> Probably the best for now is to not keep the intermediate values and to
> not thin. I don't don't don't want to have weights kicking around with
> our samples, that's for sure!

I don't understand where weights would come in.
If we would otherwise have generated five samples,
thinned to one, and returned it, we could return the
average of the samples. It's not that much extra work
algorithmically.

Do we need weighted averages if we average within
the leapfrog algorithm? If we averaged in NUTS, that
would avoid having to sample one of the points along
the tractory, right? I need to go read Radford's paper.

- Bob

If we set the maximum number of steps to something
too small, the danger we face is that the algorithm
will give the appearance of sampling just fine, but will
actually have random walk behavior.  A bigger danger is
that the convergence diagnostics will think everything is
OK in this situation.  I could easily see that happening
given the Metropolis example in the NUTS paper.

I'm not sure we're in that big of a danger of a random walk behavior with steps on the order of thousands unless the step-size is miniscule.  Even Langevin Monte Carlo avoids the worst of the Metropolis Hastings random walk behavior with just a single step.

If the model is well behaved, there's no problem with
a large number of steps because we'll never get that far.

True, but given that it's trivial to specify improper priors in stan, there are certainly ways for the simulation to go off on very long tangents without ever meeting the U-turn condition.  Although I guess this goes back to the standard bugs disclaimer: "Beware: MCMC sampling can be dangerous!"

If we set the number of steps to something small,
we'll definitely need send up red flags when we don't hit
the U-turn condition in NUTS.  That way, at least
the user would know something's going wrong.  In fact, we
should do this either way, because even 64K steps may
be too few in some situations (hey, we wanted to run
very complex models -- they may still be pretty slow).
And it'll be a good diagnostic to see.

I agree.  The number of steps taken, how often the depth limit is hit and so on are good heuristic diagnostics to report so that users can be aware of potential problems maybe go back to double check their model.

It would certainly be possible to average the samples under
   thinning rather than just returning one -- my understanding
   (from something I recall reading in the MCMC Handbook)
   is that this should improve the effective sample size
   (at least for estimating the mean).

If you're thinning then it's not worth doing this, as the trajectory
will be less useful than the thinned samples. On the flip side, since
the NUTS trajectories tend to be long, there seems to be less cause to
thin in which case the simulation trajectory could provide some useful
information.

Probably the best for now is to not keep the intermediate values and to
not thin. I don't don't don't want to have weights kicking around with
our samples, that's for sure!

I don't understand where weights would come in.
If we would otherwise have generated five samples,
thinned to one, and returned it, we could return the
average of the samples.  It's not that much extra work
algorithmically.
I think we want to avoid averaging within samples.  It's not always true that averaging even makes sense for some state-spaces.

Do we need weighted averages if we average within
the leapfrog algorithm?  If we averaged in NUTS, that
would avoid having to sample one of the points along
the tractory, right?  I need to go read Radford's paper.

The weights come in as follows:

The standard Monte Carlo estimator of a function f is

E[f(x)] ~= N^-1 \sum_i f(x_i)

Now, assume that x^(1)_i, ..., x^(L)_i is the simulation trajectory starting at sample x_i and that each point along the trajectory had a probability of being selected as the next state which is w^(1)_i, ..., w^(L)_i.  Then the following is also an estimator which has lower variance:

E[f(x)] ~= N^-1 \sum_i \sum_j w^(j)_i f(x^(j)_i)

You're effectively integrating over the choice of the next sample in the estimator instead of only using the one that was chosen when generating the chain.  In traditional HMC it means that you can even use rejected states so long as they're weighted it properly.

The down side of this is that you end up with many more samples and need to do the bookkeeping to keep track of (and use) sample weights which, as Andrew has pointed out, can be a bit tedious and annoying.

At any rate, I'm not sure how we got this far onto this tangent.  Doing this is, at best, a nice-to-have option for stan but certainly isn't necessary.

Cheers,
Marcus
